title: Tech Stock Sell-Off: Down 13%, Is Microsoft a Buy Now? - The Globe and Mail
content: Microsoft spent $45.2 billion on capex last quarter, yet free cash flow remained positive at $18.6 billion. Azure revenue grew 48%, and the commercial backlog reached $677 billion, indicating continued demand. Subscriptions to Microsoft 365 and its Copilot AI add-ons provide recurring revenue that helps fund the AI push. Tech stocks have been hit hard this month as investors worry about the enormous amount of money being spent on artificial intelligence (AI), and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) has been no exception. Shares are down about 13% from their all-time highs. But I think Microsoft is being unfairly punished here. While many big tech companies are free cash flow negative due to heavy AI spending, Microsoft has affirmed it will remain in the black at least through fiscal 2027. Missed AI’s "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we’re only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » That's a big deal. And I think it's one reason why the tech sell-off in November presents an attractive buying opportunity for Microsoft before the end of 2026. Microsoft is one of the biggest players in the cloud computing space, holding 21% of the global cloud infrastructure market. That makes Azure the second-largest provider of cloud services behind Amazon(NASDAQ:AMZN). In Microsoft's fiscal first quarter of 2027, which ended Sept. 30, Azure revenue increased 48% from the previous year. Total Microsoft Cloud revenue was $63.9 billion, up 30% from a year ago, and the company's commercial backlog reached $677 billion. That's an enormous amount of business coming down the line, so Microsoft is spending freely to ensure it has enough computing capacity to meet demand. It spent $45.2 billion on capex in the quarter. But even with that spending, free cash flow remained positive at $18.6 billion. That's because Microsoft generated $58 billion in operating cash flow during the quarter, up 29% from a year earlier. That's a big difference from some other tech companies whose AI spending has pushed free cash flow into negative territory. Despite concerns about AI spending, Microsoft's underlying business is performing very well, thanks to its well-known software business. Nearly 4 million companies use Microsoft 365, including its popular office programs such as Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and Outlook. Those subscriptions provide recurring revenue, while Microsoft's Copilot AI products provide opportunities to sell more services to existing customers. Microsoft 365 commercial cloud revenue increased 17% during the quarter. That helped Microsoft's fiscal first-quarter revenue increase 19% to $92.3 billion, while operating income climbed 21% to $45.9 billion. Net income was $36.6 billion, up 32% from a year ago. I don't expect Microsoft to slow its AI investments anytime soon -- and why should it? Microsoft Azure is generating substantial revenue, and Microsoft can continue to invest in the business while maintaining positive free cash flow. Now down 13% from its all-time high, Microsoft offers investors an opportunity to buy a highly profitable company with two powerful businesses -- cloud computing and productivity software. I think the market is overlooking Microsoft's ability to finance its AI ambitions, and it's an appealing opportunity for investors before year-end. title: Microsoft (MSFT) Is One of the Safest Ways to Own AI - The Globe and Mail
content: Microsoft (MSFT) seems to be one of the safest ways to invest in artificial intelligence (AI). The cloud and software giant posted $45.9 billion in operating income in Q1 2027. I believe that gives it considerable room to fund its next stage of growth. CEO Satya Nadella recently remarked, “We think of Copilot as the new OS for work.” I like that ambition, but I also like the existing business behind it. Following the recent tech sell-off we’ve seen in the past few weeks, Microsoft’s valuation makes that combination especially appealing. Thus, I rate MSFT stock a Buy. While “safer” is relative in tech and MSFT stock is certainly not immune to sharp pullbacks, Microsoft has built multiple ways to win as enterprises adopt AI. Rather than betting the company on a single breakthrough, it relies on cash-flowing legacy subscriptions to fund a full-stack AI ecosystem. At the infrastructure layer, Azure sells the raw computing capacity needed to train and run AI, while custom in-house silicon alongside third-party processors from Nvidia (NVDA) and AMD (AMD) reduces its reliance on any single chipmaker. Microsoft 365 Copilot embeds AI into daily office workflows, GitHub Copilot monetizes software developers, and its cybersecurity suite protects the resulting data. If rollout in one area slows, it still has several other growth engines that can pick up the slack. In addition, I view its approach to models as quite appealing. Copilot’s Auto mode automatically routes user prompts to whichever model offers the best balance of speed, capability, and cost for a given task. Similarly, Microsoft Foundry acts as an enterprise storefront offering Microsoft’s proprietary models alongside rivals like OpenAI, Anthropic, and competing providers. This also includes open models. Microsoft can therefore earn from usage even when customers switch model suppliers. At its Ignite conference in November, Microsoft pushed Copilot further into practical work. The company rolled out a unified starting hub in Copilot that merges Chat for quick queries with Cowork for longer, multi-step projects, while preparing a broad rollout of Copilot Code in the coming weeks so everyday employees can build custom apps without writing code. At the same time, Microsoft rolled out governance and data tools designed to monetize the infrastructure around AI agents. Updates to Agent 365 help IT teams manage permissions and track return on investment across both Microsoft and third-party agents, while Microsoft IQ links those agents to a company’s internal knowledge and workflows. As corporate AI usage scales, these supporting layers become increasingly sticky. So I think Microsoft can earn from the work happening around a model, even if it doesn’t produce every winning model itself. The latest quarter shows it working already for Microsoft. In its Fiscal Q1 2027 results, Microsoft’s revenue grew 19% year-over-year to $92.3 billion. Operating income increased 21% to $45.9 billion, while adjusted earnings per share (EPS) rose 18% to $4.89. Microsoft Cloud revenue climbed 30% to $63.9 billion. Azure accelerated to 48% growth, with guidance for 49%–50% constant-currency growth this quarter. That suggests customers are already using the capacity Microsoft is building. Moreover, adoption figures are encouraging. Daily Copilot users increased nearly 50% sequentially and more than fivefold year-over-year. Customers with over 50,000 Copilot seats increased more than eightfold year-over-year. Copilot revenue growth also accelerated sequentially. Foundry passed 120,000 customers, with revenue more than tripling year-over-year. Customers building agentic applications with multiple models increased fivefold year-over-year. I believe these figures suggest broader deployment, with large organizations committing to substantial usage. Volkswagen’s (VWAGY) planned rollout to over 330,000 employees is one example. Microsoft also has $677 billion in remaining commercial performance obligations. This provides excellent visibility into future revenue. Operating cash flow reached $58 billion, leaving $18.6 billion of free cash flow after cash investment. So that gives it considerable internal funding for expansion. Note that enterprises are still early in putting agents into production. Yet Microsoft already supplies much of their software and identity infrastructure. Selling additional capabilities to those customers should be easier than building those relationships from scratch. Now, the recent sell-off has pushed MSFT’s valuation to rather attractive levels, in my view. Today, MSFT trades at 24.59x Fiscal 2027 consensus EPS of $20.03. That falls to 20.33x Fiscal 2028 EPS of $24.23 and 16.31x Fiscal 2029 EPS of $30.20. Consensus expects roughly 16% EPS growth this year, followed by nearly 21% and 25%. I find those multiples exceptional for a business with Microsoft’s recurring revenue and profitability. The estimates may also leave room for further upside. Adjusted EPS of $4.89 beat the latest $4.72 forecast. The preceding quarter delivered $4.74 against $4.24 expected. Repeated beats don’t promise more, but they make me reluctant to assume consensus captures the full earnings opportunity. Azure’s acceleration and wider Copilot adoption could keep driving upgrades. Delivering today’s estimates alone would bring the multiple toward 16.31x by Fiscal 2029. So I don’t think strong returns would rely on an aggressive rerating. Lastly, I should mention that investors are right to question returns on enormous AI spending. Microsoft’s quarterly capex reached $45.2 billion, including finance leases. Competition from Amazon (AMZN) and Google (GOOGL) remains intense, and other enterprise AI platforms are also competing for customers. Infrastructure costs could pressure cloud margins, and Copilot adoption might slow. Sustaining 20%-plus earnings growth also becomes harder at Microsoft’s size. However, today’s cloud growth and cash generation give me more confidence in the spending. Its AI business is already producing revenue across several products. Wall Street rates MSFT a Strong Buy, based on 35 Buys and four Holds. The $632.48 average price target implies roughly 28% upside from today’s price levels. Microsoft offers AI exposure without requiring one model or application to dominate. Its existing businesses fund the expansion, while Azure and Copilot already show substantial demand. Ignite adds more ways to earn from enterprise agents. At roughly 20.33x Fiscal 2028 earnings, I think the sell-off has created an attractive entry point for what could be one of the safest companies to own AI. I remain Bullish. © Copyright 2026 The Globe and Mail Inc. All rights reserved.

Coinbase pays us for certain activity generated through this link. Prices displayed are informational. Microsoft (MSFT) seems to be one of the safest ways to invest in artificial intelligence (AI). The cloud and software giant posted $45.9 billion in operating income in Q1 2027. I believe that gives it considerable room to fund its next stage of growth. CEO Satya Nadella recently remarked, "We think of Copilot as the new OS for work." I like that ambition, but I also like the existing business behind it. Following the recent tech sell-off we've seen in the past few weeks, Microsoft's valuation makes that combination especially appealing. Thus, I rate MSFT stock a Buy. While "safer" is relative in tech and MSFT stock is certainly not immune to sharp pullbacks, Microsoft has built multiple ways to win as enterprises adopt AI. Rather than betting the company on a single breakthrough, it relies on cash-flowing legacy subscriptions to fund a full-stack AI ecosystem. At the infrastructure layer, Azure sells the raw computing capacity needed to train and run AI, while custom in-house silicon alongside third-party processors from Nvidia (NVDA) and AMD (AMD) reduces its reliance on any single chipmaker. Microsoft 365 Copilot embeds AI into daily office workflows, GitHub Copilot monetizes software developers, and its cybersecurity suite protects the resulting data. If rollout in one area slows, it still has several other growth engines that can pick up the slack. In addition, I view its approach to models as quite appealing. Copilot's Auto mode automatically routes user prompts to whichever model offers the best balance of speed, capability, and cost for a given task. Similarly, Microsoft Foundry acts as an enterprise storefront offering Microsoft's proprietary models alongside rivals like OpenAI, Anthropic, and competing providers. This also includes open models. Microsoft can therefore earn from usage even when customers switch model suppliers. At its Ignite conference in November, Microsoft pushed Copilot further into practical work. The company rolled out a unified starting hub in Copilot that merges Chat for quick queries with Cowork for longer, multi-step projects, while preparing a broad rollout of Copilot Code in the coming weeks so everyday employees can build custom apps without writing code. At the same time, Microsoft rolled out governance and data tools designed to monetize the infrastructure around AI agents. Updates to Agent 365 help IT teams manage permissions and track return on investment across both Microsoft and third-party agents, while Microsoft IQ links those agents to a company's internal knowledge and workflows. As corporate AI usage scales, these supporting layers become increasingly sticky. So I think Microsoft can earn from the work happening around a model, even if it doesn't produce every winning model itself. The latest quarter shows it working already for Microsoft. In its Fiscal Q1 2027 results, Microsoft's revenue grew 19% year-over-year to $92.3 billion. Operating income increased 21% to $45.9 billion, while adjusted earnings per share (EPS) rose 18% to $4.89. Microsoft Cloud revenue climbed 30% to $63.9 billion. Azure accelerated to 48% growth, with guidance for 49%–50% constant-currency growth this quarter. That suggests customers are already using the capacity Microsoft is building. Moreover, adoption figures are encouraging. Daily Copilot users increased nearly 50% sequentially and more than fivefold year-over-year. Customers with over 50,000 Copilot seats increased more than eightfold year-over-year. Copilot revenue growth also accelerated sequentially. Foundry passed 120,000 customers, with revenue more than tripling year-over-year. Customers building agentic applications with multiple models increased fivefold year-over-year. I believe these figures suggest broader deployment, with large organizations committing to substantial usage. Volkswagen's (VWAGY) planned rollout to over 330,000 employees is one example. Microsoft also has $677 billion in remaining commercial performance obligations. This provides excellent visibility into future revenue. Operating cash flow reached $58 billion, leaving $18.6 billion of free cash flow after cash investment. So that gives it considerable internal funding for expansion. Note that enterprises are still early in putting agents into production. Yet Microsoft already supplies much of their software and identity infrastructure. Selling additional capabilities to those customers should be easier than building those relationships from scratch. Now, the recent sell-off has pushed MSFT's valuation to rather attractive levels, in my view. Today, MSFT trades at 24.59x Fiscal 2027 consensus EPS of $20.03. That falls to 20.33x Fiscal 2028 EPS of $24.23 and 16.31x Fiscal 2029 EPS of $30.20. Consensus expects roughly 16% EPS growth this year, followed by nearly 21% and 25%. I find those multiples exceptional for a business with Microsoft's recurring revenue and profitability. The estimates may also leave room for further upside. Adjusted EPS of $4.89 beat the latest $4.72 forecast. The preceding quarter delivered $4.74 against $4.24 expected. Repeated beats don't promise more, but they make me reluctant to assume consensus captures the full earnings opportunity. Azure's acceleration and wider Copilot adoption could keep driving upgrades. Delivering today's estimates alone would bring the multiple toward 16.31x by Fiscal 2029. So I don't think strong returns would rely on an aggressive rerating. Lastly, I should mention that investors are right to question returns on enormous AI spending. Microsoft's quarterly capex reached $45.2 billion, including finance leases. Competition from Amazon (AMZN) and Google (GOOGL) remains intense, and other enterprise AI platforms are also competing for customers. Infrastructure costs could pressure cloud margins, and Copilot adoption might slow. Sustaining 20%-plus earnings growth also becomes harder at Microsoft's size. However, today's cloud growth and cash generation give me more confidence in the spending. Its AI business is already producing revenue across several products. Wall Street rates MSFT a Strong Buy, based on 35 Buys and four Holds. The $632.48 average price target implies roughly 28% upside from today's price levels. Microsoft offers AI exposure without requiring one model or application to dominate. Its existing businesses fund the expansion, while Azure and Copilot already show substantial demand. Ignite adds more ways to earn from enterprise agents. At roughly 20.33x Fiscal 2028 earnings, I think the sell-off has created an attractive entry point for what could be one of the safest companies to own AI. I remain Bullish. title: Microsoft Stock Jumps In Nvidia-Fueled Tech Surge; Is Microsoft A Buy Now? - Investor's Business Daily
content: Microsoft  (MSFT)stock joined a larger tech-led relief rally Monday while remaining below a key chart level. Major technology stocks, including Microsoft, spiked up after Nvidia (NVDA) said it's bringing back co-founder Jensen Huang to his position as the chipmaker's chief executive. Shares of Microsoft broke out of a cup base at a pivot of 466.32 amid a four-day winning streak in August and hit an all-time high of 559.15 on Nov. 4. On Monday, the shares rose nearly 2% but were still 11% below their high. The software maker's stock came under pressure recently after businesses and individuals were affected by a global outage of Microsoft's Outlook and Microsoft 365 products. The tech industry heavyweight on Nov. 14 said its Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook and Teams, were fully restored in the wake of a worldwide outage. No malicious activity or disruptions due to artificial intelligence were reported. Microsoft said the outage occurred because of a latent bug issue that caused servers to become unresponsive under certain loads. Meanwhile, on Nov. 10, Anthropic (ANT) announced a beta launch of Claude Sheets, a direct challenge to Microsoft's Excel program. Investors had a sense of deja vu, recalling when releases related to Anthropic's Claude Code sent software stocks, including Microsoft, tumbling earlier this year. Shares fell 2.2% on the day and had been making new lows coming into Monday. Still, Microsoft's Relative Strength Rating sits at 81, just above the 80 threshold recommended by Investor's Business Daily. That marks a commendable achievement after last week's tech wreck that sent the Nasdaq composite down 8.6%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average component delivered an earnings beat for its fiscal first quarter. Profit of $4.89 a share exceeded Wall Street's target of $4.71 a share in results released Oct. 28. Revenue grew 19% to $92.3 billion, also topping views of $90.6 billion. Earnings increased 18% from the prior year. The results also beat Microsoft's own internal forecast of $90.4 billion in sales. Growth in its cloud-based service Azure reached 48%, accelerating from a 43% increase in the fiscal fourth quarter. That performance, along with technical strength and outperformance in other criteria, has earned Microsoft stock a Composite Rating of 95 out of 99. Meanwhile, for Microsoft's fiscal 2027 – which started on July 1 – Wall Street is looking for a 16% earnings increase to $20.08 a share. In 2028, analysts project a 20% rise to $24.10 a share.
